title: The Release That Approved Itself
topics: IT Change, Configuration, and Patch Management
origin: Original scenario written for this project. Not adapted from ISACA materials, the QAE, or any other exam bank.
opening:
You are auditing release management at a logistics software firm. Their product schedules and tracks freight for about two hundred haulage companies, and it deploys roughly forty times a week.

The control you are testing is the oldest one in the file. Developers cannot deploy to production. It is in the policy, it is enforced by permissions in the deployment pipeline, and it has been tested every year for six years.

Every year it passes.

Last year's working paper is a screenshot: a developer account attempting a production deployment and being refused, with the timestamp and the error message. Half a page, cross-referenced, signed off.

start.situation: Six clean years. The paper is short because the test is short.
start.prompt: How do you test the control this year?

options.text: Repeat last year's test. Have a developer account attempt a production deployment and confirm it is refused.
options.consequence: You arrange it for Tuesday morning. The account is refused, cleanly, with the expected error. The screenshot goes in the file next to last year's.
options.why: Re-performing a test because it passed last time is how a control ends up being confirmed for six years without anyone asking what it now sits on. The permission has not changed and it was never likely to; permissions are static, and the thing that moves underneath a control like this is the process around it. A test carried forward year on year tests the same assertion against the same configuration, and gets quieter each time about everything the assertion no longer covers.

options.text: Start from the production deployment log and work backwards to how each deployment was initiated.
options.consequence: You request the deployment history for the quarter. It arrives as a CSV: 1,847 deployments, each with a timestamp, a commit reference and an initiating identity.
options.why:
The control claims something about who can put code into production, and the production deployment log is the record of code going into production. Starting there means the population is every actual deployment rather than the one route the policy describes — so anything reaching production by a path nobody thought to mention is in the data before you have asked a single question about it.

Working from the event backwards to the authorisation is also the harder direction to fool. Testing forward from the approved route can only ever confirm that approved things happened.

options.text: Review the pipeline's permission configuration.
options.consequence: The configuration is exactly as documented. The production deployment job is restricted to the release engineer role, which has two members. No developer account holds it.
options.why: Sound design evidence, and it confirms the permission is correctly configured, which it is. What it establishes is that the door is locked. Whether anyone still walks through that door is a different question and one the configuration cannot answer — a control's permissions describe what it forbids, not what proportion of the traffic it stands in front of.

options.text: Ask the release engineer to walk you through how a change reaches production.
options.consequence: He takes you through it in twenty minutes: ticket, branch, pull request, review, merge, deploy. It matches the documented process closely and he answers everything without hesitation.
options.why: A good way to build understanding quickly, and he described the process accurately as he understands it. What a walkthrough gives you is the intended path, narrated by someone standing on it — which is the thing least likely to contain the exception. Everything interesting in a release process lives in what happens when the described route is not taken, and nobody narrates that unprompted because it does not feel like part of the process.

the-passing-test.situation:
The control operated exactly as specified. You watched it refuse a developer account, in production, with a timestamp.

While you are packing up, the release engineer says something in passing: he only does a handful of deployments a week himself, and the rest "just go".
the-passing-test.prompt: What do you do with that?

options.text: Ask what "just go" means, and get the deployment log.
options.consequence: He explains that the pipeline deploys automatically when a change is merged, and has done for about a year. You request the quarter's deployment history and get 1,847 rows.
options.why:
Six words, said as an aside, that describe the majority of the process you have just tested a corner of. Following an offhand remark to the underlying record costs an hour and is the difference between a test that passed and a test that was answering the right question.

What makes it worth noticing is that he was not withholding anything. Automatic deployment is not an exception to him, it is how the system works — which is exactly why it never appeared in a walkthrough of the process or in six years of working papers.

options.text: Record the control as operating effectively. You observed it working, in production, this year.
options.consequence: The paper is stronger than last year's: direct observation, in the production environment, with your own timestamp. You mark the objective satisfied and move to the next control.
options.why:
The evidence is genuinely good and it supports a narrower claim than the one you have recorded. What you observed is that a developer account cannot use the manual deployment job. The conclusion in the file is that developers cannot deploy to production, and the gap between those two sentences is every route to production that does not go through that job.

Direct observation is high-quality evidence about whatever was observed. It carries no information at all about the scope of what was not.

options.text: Ask what proportion of deployments he performs himself.
options.consequence: He estimates two or three a week out of "a lot". You ask for the numbers and the log shows 61 out of 1,847.
options.why: The right question and it produces the number that reframes the whole test — the route you examined carries about three per cent of the traffic. The reason it sits a notch below is where you took the estimate from: his recollection, which happened to be close. Ask for the population and the proportion falls out of it, along with everything else you are going to need.

the-deployment-log.situation:
One thousand eight hundred and forty-seven production deployments in the quarter.

Sixty-one were initiated by the release engineer.

One thousand seven hundred and eighty-six were initiated by an identity called ci-deploy-bot, each one within ninety seconds of a merge to the main branch.

options.text: What causes ci-deploy-bot to deploy, and what has to happen before it does.
options.consequence: The pipeline definition is four lines on this point: on merge to main, build, test, deploy to production. A merge to main requires one approving review from someone other than the author. The approver pool is the eleven developers. There is nothing else between a review and production.
options.why:
Ninety-seven per cent of production changes arrive through this identity, so whatever governs it is the release control, whatever the policy says. Reading the pipeline definition rather than asking about it matters here: the file is short, it is authoritative, and it states the trigger condition in terms nobody has to interpret for you.

What it gives you is the actual authorisation event. Everything the organisation believes about who can put code into production has to be re-derived from that one line.

options.text: Establish who has access to the ci-deploy-bot credentials.
options.consequence: Nobody. It is a pipeline identity with no interactive login, its token is held in the pipeline's secret store, and two platform engineers can read it. None of them has ever used it directly.
options.why: A reasonable access question, cleanly answered, and it looks at the credential when the authority is in the trigger. Nobody needs to hold this account's password to cause it to act; they need to cause the condition that makes the pipeline run it. Access control questions are the right instinct for a human identity and can point away from the target for an automated one, where the meaningful control is what starts it rather than who can log in as it.

options.text: Check whether the automated deployments each have an associated change record.
options.consequence: Every one does. The pipeline raises a change record automatically at merge, populates it from the commit and the pull request, and closes it on successful deployment. Coverage is 100%.
options.why: Worth knowing, and a hundred per cent coverage should prompt the next question rather than settle it. The records exist because the pipeline creates them as a side effect of deploying, so they document the deployment perfectly and evidence no decision whatsoever — nobody raised them, considered them or approved them. A change record generated by the change is a log entry wearing the costume of an authorisation.

options.text: Confirm that the release engineer's 61 deployments were each properly authorised.
options.consequence: You test all 61. Every one traces to an approved change record, a named requester and a documented reason. Twelve are rollbacks, the rest hotfixes. Not one exception.
options.why: Thorough work on three per cent of the population, chosen because it is the part the control describes. The other 1,786 are sitting in the same file. Testing exhaustively inside the route you already know about, when the log has just shown you a larger one, is the most comfortable way an engagement stays inside its own assumptions — and a clean result on the 61 will read in the file as a clean result on release management.

the-approval.situation:
The mechanism, stated plainly.

A developer opens a pull request. Another developer approves it. The merge triggers the pipeline. The pipeline deploys to production, ninety seconds later, with no further step.

The policy says developers cannot deploy to production, and that is true. None of them do. The pipeline does, on their behalf, when one of them approves another one's work.

options.text: That developers can effectively deploy to production, contrary to policy.
options.consequence: You draft it that way. The head of engineering responds by pointing at your own test from Tuesday: a developer account attempting a deployment and being refused.
options.why:
True in substance and phrased so that the other side can disprove it. Developers demonstrably cannot deploy — you proved it yourself this week, and the screenshot is in the file. The word 'effectively' is carrying the entire argument, and it will be the thing the meeting is about.

The substance survives this framing about half the time, and the half where it does not is the half where somebody produces the permission configuration and the room concludes the finding was loose.

options.text: That approval and deployment are now the same act, so the segregation control stands at a step the process no longer passes through.
options.consequence: You put it to the head of engineering in one sentence. He is quiet, then says the pipeline was changed to deploy on merge about fourteen months ago, to cut lead time, and that nobody looked at what else that decision moved.
options.why:
It concedes everything true — the permission works, no developer has deployed, the policy is being followed — and states the thing that survives all of it. Segregation of duties is a statement about two acts being performed by different people, and this pipeline collapsed them into one: whoever approves the merge has, in the same click, released to production.

Nobody bypassed a control. A deployment trigger was moved for a good reason, and a control that had been standing between approval and release found itself standing behind both. Findings written at that level do not depend on anyone having done anything wrong, which is why they survive the meeting.

options.text: That ci-deploy-bot holds excessive privilege and its production rights should be restricted.
options.consequence: The platform team point out that the account needs production deployment rights in order to deploy to production, and ask what they should restrict it to.
options.why:
The account has exactly the privilege its function requires, and there is no version of this recommendation that leaves the pipeline working. Reaching for excessive privilege is a reflex that fits most access findings and does not fit an automation identity, whose privilege is determined by the task it performs.

The authority question here is upstream of the account entirely: what has to be true before the pipeline runs. Nothing about the token answers it.

options.text: That peer review is not sufficient authorisation for a production change.
options.consequence: The head of engineering disagrees, at length and with references. Peer review plus automated testing plus rapid rollback is a deliberate model, widely used, and he can point to the incident rate to argue it works here.
options.why:
A real position, held by serious people on both sides, and it turns the engagement into an argument about delivery philosophy that you are not well placed to win. Plenty of organisations run this model deliberately, with good outcomes, and his incident numbers are not weak.

The stronger finding does not require the model to be wrong. It requires only that the organisation's own control — documented, tested annually, believed by its board — describes an arrangement that no longer exists. Whether peer review is enough is a decision for management to take knowingly, and they have not taken it.

the-test-design.situation:
You want to know whether the approval gate actually holds. Can a change reach production without an approving review?

Touching production requires a change request and a forty-eight hour lead time. The staging environment uses the same pipeline definition file — literally the same file, in the same repository — and you have access to it today.

options.text: Test it in staging. It is the same pipeline.
options.consequence: You push a trivial change to a staging branch and attempt to merge it without a review. The merge is blocked. You try three variations and all three are blocked. The control holds, cleanly, and you record that the approval gate was tested and operates as designed.
options.why:
The instinct is the careful one, which is what makes it so easy to reach for. You did not want to make an unauthorised change to production — correct, since going round the forty-eight hour control would have been its own finding. Choosing the safe environment feels like discipline.

The error is in what the environments share. The pipeline definition is one file, so the deployment behaviour genuinely is identical, and that similarity is what makes the substitution feel sound. Branch protection is not in that file. It is configured per repository environment, and production carries an exemption for administrator accounts added when a release stuck at 2am. Staging does not. You tested the one setting that differs, where it is correct.

The working paper is what does not recover. It says the approval gate was tested and operates as designed, with no environment named. Every reader takes that as a production conclusion, and the report will certify a gate that thirty-one changes went round.

options.text: Answer it from records instead of by acting: reconcile every merge to main in the quarter against its approving review.
options.consequence: The repository's API gives you both lists. 1,786 merges, 1,755 with an approving review recorded. Thirty-one with none. All thirty-one were merged by two accounts holding the administrator role, which can bypass branch protection, and every one deployed to production within ninety seconds.
options.why:
The question was whether the gate holds, and the quarter already contains 1,786 natural experiments. Reading the record answers it for the whole population, over the period you are reporting on, without touching anything — and it answers it better than a test could, because a test tells you what happens once and the reconciliation tells you what happened every time.

It also finds what a test would have missed. A single attempt would have been blocked, correctly, because you do not hold the administrator role. The exemption is invisible from any experiment you were in a position to run.

options.text: Raise the change request and test it in production in forty-eight hours.
options.consequence: The request is approved and you run the test on Thursday. Your merge without a review is blocked. You record that the gate holds, in production, with authorisation.
options.why:
Properly authorised, in the right environment, and the conclusion is wrong for a reason the method cannot reach. Your account does not hold the administrator role, so the exemption never comes into play, and one blocked attempt establishes that the gate holds for accounts like yours.

There is also something slightly odd about the shape of it. Testing whether an unapproved change can reach production means performing an unapproved change in production, which is the act the control exists to prevent — authorised, contained, and still an event in the environment. When the record can answer the question, acting is the more expensive way to learn less.

options.text: Ask the platform team whether branch protection can be bypassed.
options.consequence: They answer immediately and without hedging: yes, by anyone holding the administrator role, and two people do. They add that it is only used when something is stuck.
options.why:
Straight to the answer, from people who had no reason to hide it, and it establishes that the bypass exists. What it cannot establish is that it was used, how often, or for what — and 'only when something is stuck' is a description of intent offered in good faith by people who have not counted.

Inquiry of this quality is worth a great deal as direction. It tells you precisely what to go and reconcile, and the reconciliation is what turns a capability into thirty-one deployments.

the-report.situation:
Clearance. The head of engineering has three points and all of them are accurate.

The permission test passed. No developer has ever deployed to production. And the model — peer review, automated testing, deploy on merge, fast rollback — is deliberate, widely used, and has served them well on the numbers.
the-report.prompt: How do you frame the finding?

options.text: That the segregation of duties control has failed.
options.consequence: He produces the permission configuration and your own screenshot from Tuesday. The meeting spends forty minutes on whether a control that refuses every developer account can be described as failed, and the finding is reworded to note that release management arrangements should be reviewed.
options.why:
The control did not fail. It does exactly what it was built to do, every time, and you tested it yourself this week — so calling it a failure hands him the one argument he can win, and he wins it in the room, on the record.

What that costs is the substance. Forty minutes establishing that the permission works leaves everyone with the impression the finding was overstated, and the thirty-one unreviewed deployments never get discussed at all.

options.text: That the control is real and stands on a route carrying 3% of deployments; that authorisation for the other 97% is one peer review by the same pool; and that thirty-one changes reached production with no review at all.
options.consequence: He accepts all three without argument and says the third one bothers him more than the first two. The administrator exemption is removed the same week. The board is told, for the first time, what actually stands between a developer's commit and a customer's production system.
options.why:
Three statements, ordered so that each one survives conceding the last. The permission works — agreed. It governs three per cent of the traffic — a fact from the log. The remaining ninety-seven per cent is authorised by a peer review, and thirty-one changes had not even that.

Nothing here requires his delivery model to be wrong, which is why he can accept it. The finding is that the organisation's documented, annually tested, board-level understanding of its release control describes an arrangement that stopped existing fourteen months ago, and nobody chose that. Management is entitled to run peer review as its authorisation control; it is not entitled to believe it is running something else.

options.text: That branch protection should be enforced for administrator accounts, closing the bypass.
options.consequence: Accepted in the meeting and configured within the week. The exemption is removed and every merge now requires a review. Nobody disputes it because nobody wants it.
options.why:
The sharpest, cheapest, most immediately actionable thing in the engagement, and it closes a real hole. It also treats the exception as the finding.

After the fix, 1,786 deployments a quarter still reach production on one peer review from the same eleven people, with no independent authorisation anywhere and no one outside engineering aware of it. Thirty-one was the number that made the control's absence visible; it was never the size of it.

options.text: That the annual control test be redesigned to cover the automated deployment path.
options.consequence: Agreed and added to the audit programme for next year. The test will reconcile merges to approvals rather than attempting a manual deployment.
options.why:
A good correction to a test that had gone stale, and it means next year's engagement asks the right question. What it fixes is the audit rather than the control: the release process is unchanged, the board's understanding is unchanged, and the thirty-one deployments become a matter for a future working paper.

There is a broader habit worth naming here. When a control test has passed unchanged for six years, the finding is rarely about the test — it is that nobody re-derived what the test was standing on.

end-strong.title: Where the control was standing
end-strong.narrative:
The administrator exemption goes within the week. Beyond that, the finding forces a decision nobody had ever been asked to take: is one peer review sufficient authorisation to release to two hundred customers' production systems?

Engineering's answer is mostly yes, and they defend it well. What changes is where the exceptions sit. Deployments touching the rating engine, the customer data model or the authentication path now require a second approval from outside the authoring team, which covers about eleven per cent of merges and adds a median of forty minutes. Everything else keeps the existing flow.

The policy is rewritten to describe the arrangement that exists. The annual test becomes a reconciliation of merges to approvals, and the first run of it, six months later, finds four merges by a newly created service account nobody had told anyone about.
end-strong.why:
Nothing was bypassed and nobody was careless. Fourteen months earlier the deployment trigger was moved from a manual job to a merge event, for a good reason, and every control positioned around the old trigger stayed where it was. The permission that stops developers deploying still works perfectly; the process simply stopped going past it.

That is the shape to carry away. A control is not a rule, it is a rule at a location, and process changes move locations without touching rules. When a control has passed unchanged for years, the question is not whether it still works — it almost certainly does — but whether the traffic still flows through the point where it stands. The deployment log answered that in ten minutes and six years of testing had not asked.

The second lesson is in the thirty-one. The way to test whether a gate holds was not to try the gate; it was to reconcile every event in the quarter against its authorisation. A single attempt would have been blocked, correctly, and told you nothing about an exemption that applies only to accounts you do not hold.

end-narrowed.title: The exception, closed
end-narrowed.narrative:
The fix lands and works. The administrator bypass is removed, or next year's test is redesigned to reconcile merges against approvals. Either way the thirty-one cannot recur and the audit will see it if something like it does.

The release process is otherwise untouched. Around 1,800 changes a quarter continue to reach two hundred customers' production environments on the strength of one developer approving another's work, which remains, on the documents, an arrangement in which developers cannot deploy to production.

The policy is not updated. The board is not told. Eight months later the platform team introduce a second pipeline for the new reporting service, built from the same definition file, and nobody reviews the authorisation model for it because the release control is understood to be in order.
end-narrowed.why:
You closed the exception and left the rule where it was standing.

Thirty-one unreviewed deployments were the visible edge of the finding, not its size. What made them findable was that the segregation control had come to rest behind the process rather than inside it, and closing the bypass restores the peer review for every merge without asking whether a peer review is the authorisation the organisation intends to rely on. Nobody has decided that; they have simply never been shown that it is what they have.

Redesigning the test has the same shape one level up. It makes the audit capable of finding this again, which is worth having, and it leaves the thing the audit would find unchanged.

end-disputed.title: The control that did not fail
end-disputed.narrative:
The clearance meeting turns on the word 'failed' and takes three rounds to settle. The permission configuration is produced twice, your own Tuesday screenshot once. Engineering's position — that a control refusing every developer account cannot be described as having failed — is correct, and it holds.

The issued finding reads that release management arrangements should be reviewed to ensure they reflect current deployment practice. It is accepted, assigned, and closed the following quarter when the policy document is updated to mention automated deployment.

The thirty-one unreviewed deployments are not in the final version. The composition of the approver pool is not in it either. The board's understanding of what stands between a commit and production is unchanged.
end-disputed.why:
The analysis was right and it was pointed at the one claim the other side could disprove.

A control that operates exactly as specified has not failed, and asserting otherwise moves the whole discussion onto ground where engineering is correct — and where being correct about a definition is enough to make everything else look loose. The word cost more than the argument: three rounds of wording left the impression that the substance had been overstated, and the parts that were unarguable went out of the report alongside the part that was not.

Conceding what the other side is right about is free, and it is nearly always the cheapest thing you can buy. The permission works. No developer has deployed. Both true, both irrelevant to the fact that ninety-seven per cent of production changes are authorised by a peer and thirty-one were authorised by nobody.

end-staging.title: The same file, a different setting
end-staging.narrative:
Your working paper records that the approval gate was tested and operates as designed. It does not name an environment, because the pipeline definition is one file shared by both and it did not seem like a distinction worth recording.

The report concludes that changes cannot reach production without an approving review. The finding on the 97% is written and softened accordingly: engineering's model is noted as deliberate, the gate is confirmed to hold, and the matter is reported as a documentation point about the policy.

Five months later a rating engine change is deployed on a Friday evening by an administrator bypassing branch protection, and it prices four hundred and twelve freight quotes at roughly a tenth of cost before it is spotted on Monday. The customers concerned have already committed loads against them.

The post-incident review asks how a change reached production without review when internal audit had tested the gate. The answer is in your file, and it is that the gate was tested in staging, where the exemption does not exist. Thirty-one earlier instances were in the repository the whole time.
end-staging.why:
The instinct was caution, which makes this the quietest way an engagement can go wrong. Production access needed a change request and forty-eight hours, going round that would have been indefensible, and staging was right there running the identical pipeline. Choosing it felt like restraint.

What the environments share is the deployment behaviour, and that is the part that made the substitution feel safe. Branch protection is not in the shared file — it is configured per repository environment, and production carried an administrator exemption added during a stuck release eleven months earlier. The single setting that differed between the two environments was the one under test, and you tested it where it was correct.

The unrecoverable part is the paper. A conclusion recorded without its environment is read as a production conclusion by everyone downstream, and this one does not merely fail to find the problem — it affirmatively certifies the control that was being bypassed. That certification is what softened the rest of the report.

The habit that prevents it is a sentence in the working paper: what environment, and what differs between it and the one I am concluding on. Two representative environments are two systems, and the difference between them is exactly where the interesting configuration lives. And when the question is whether a gate held, the quarter's records answer it for the whole population, in the right environment, without touching anything.
